Of course your core audience and your social media and gaming board voices clearly aren’t the same thing. Just focus on running a good business, building a good product, and keeping the wagon train moving.

author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content: Anyway guys, Starbased is a problem of discrete mathematics, with N unknowns and M constraints where N represents the assets and M the possibilities. Obviously, the possibilities are not identical for every faction, but this does not imply that the optimum, understood as the intersection of various cutting planes, is worse for one faction over another. There could simply be 3 different optima. Now, I haven't calculated precisely for every possibility, after all, beyond being a purely mathematical problem, it's also a game and I see it as such too. If we want to discuss discrepancies between factions, we must also consider that we can't just add apples and oranges, or at least it's not assumed that in the overall vision, this was intended to create differences for a different gameplay.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: I'm not a fan of a mandatory withdraw tax. And the CSS->CSS is just another form of a withdraw tax. You would need a lot of fuel and a lot of time for it. Also you need to fly into hostile sectors. When we get a new instance of Labs, all would need to pay this tax when withdrawing ships (if there is no exception). Also if you want to change your wallet, e.g. from a hot wallet to a ledger wallet, you would also need to pay the tax - for ALL of your ships. Or you simply want to sell a ship, because you got a better one from the marketplace. I should pay for my own property? This is like holding a ship hostage until I pay a ransom. I would like to see the following system, where the tax is fully optional: When you withdraw a ship, it gets a new trait "Faction". If you withdrew the ship from Oni, it has "Faction: Oni". You can only import this ship in the same faction. But you can remove the faction trait in two ways: 1) wait e.g. 7 days and get the faction removed for free 2) pay a tax to get it immediately removed. So when I want to sell the ship, I have 3 options: The above two or instantly sell the ship as a Oni-pegged ship. Or make a third/alternative option (to pick up the CSS->CSS idea): 3) there is an independent CSS at sector 0,0. If you fly your ship to this CSS, you can withdraw your ship without a faction trait.

author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content: @𝒥𝑜𝓃𝒥𝑜𝓃𝟡𝟚 ☠ Every transactio in solana has a base fee of some LAMPORTS, what a transaction need is a keypair (public-private). How much a transaction cost depends only on the software you are using to sign that transaction. A wallet is just a passive entity (which is basically the keypair). If you use Phantom you have higher fees cause it add more LAMPORTS as gas fee as Priority Fee. This means you have faster transactions but higher fees. Solflare, on contrary, doesnt have priority fees so you pay less but with slower priority fees. If you enable priority fees inside Based, you basically add a layer of priority fees on top of what I explained. (which is partially true cause priority fees are calculated by SA instead of Phantom in that case)

content: Here's a RED HOT TAKE:   There will be an evolution of the Star Atlas economic model.  Most SMALL players will quit SAGE.  NOT THIS YEAR... but when the bear market comes in 2025.  It just won't be worth their time and they won't make enough to keep the grind going.  Some will... but many won't.  Only mid to large players will continue in SAGE until the next bull cycle.  Is that bad?  NOT IF... we get a solid base of UE5 players that spend $5-$20 a month on R4 and other assets.  If we get tens of thousands of people playing the racing game and buying R4.,If we get tens of thousands of players playing SURGE and buying R4., Most players will be happy to play those game modes and maybe earn or lose a few bucks a month.  Plus they will "build long term equity" in their characters/crew.  HERE IS ONE WAY THE SMALL GUYS COULD MAKE MONEY AND HAVE A BLAST: Big Game Hunting/Monster Hunting game mode.  Big Game Hunting will be the more classic "MMO mode" in Star Atlas for the foreseeable future.  How could that be profitable?  UNIQUE RESOURCES that can ONLY be gathered in that game mode: unique resources, DATA, blueprints, pills, potions, etc...  that they can sell to the bigger players for in game advantages., That will create a full circular economy between the smaller players and the bigger players.  Many of the bigger players (myself included) won't have time to grind UE5 game modes.    In short, I believe the economy will evolve into: PRODUCERS (SAGE players) and CONSUMERS (UE5 gamers). author: The Only SignalONI
content: This completely depends on:  User growth,I see some people talk about our user growth sometimes like our focus is user growth. We completely locked in on our community, spent $0 on marketing and gave our all to you guys instead. We don't have official in-game tutorials for our games and crypto is still complex to the everyday person. Given all that, of course we're not going to grow. However, that is going to change this year. We're going public access, have some marketing planned, other plans to make the crypto aspect more simple in-game etc. All that plus a (Hopefully) bull market. I think people will be surprised by our user growth when we hone in on it.  What ship production looks like,Is it infinite inflation? Do ships need to be destroyed before one can be produced? Is there an algo of active players that needs to be looked at to determine how many ships can be produced? I HAVE NO IDEA where we're going with this tbh but I think a general "When people can produce ships, ships will tank" is too early to tell.  Type of ship,I think the type of ship will hopefully contribute to what the price is. For example the VZUS Opod has some decent utility, is one of the first ships, and might have collectors value.  Utility ,There's still too many ships without utility that keep the price lower imo. An easy example is combat ships when combat is online (in sage and UE5). More utility = more people who want said ship  This is all to say I'm not really convinced ships will just tank nonstop. Some of this might seem obvious but thought I'd add my thoughts either way

content: This completely depends on:  User growth,I see some people talk about our user growth sometimes like our focus is user growth. We completely locked in on our community, spent $0 on marketing and gave our all to you guys instead. We don't have official in-game tutorials for our games and crypto is still complex to the everyday person. Given all that, of course we're not going to grow. However, that is going to change this year. We're going public access, have some marketing planned, other plans to make the crypto aspect more simple in-game etc. All that plus a (Hopefully) bull market. I think people will be surprised by our user growth when we hone in on it.  What ship production looks like,Is it infinite inflation? Do ships need to be destroyed before one can be produced? Is there an algo of active players that needs to be looked at to determine how many ships can be produced? I HAVE NO IDEA where we're going with this tbh but I think a general "When people can produce ships, ships will tank" is too early to tell.  Type of ship,I think the type of ship will hopefully contribute to what the price is. For example the VZUS Opod has some decent utility, is one of the first ships, and might have collectors value.  Utility ,There's still too many ships without utility that keep the price lower imo. An easy example is combat ships when combat is online (in sage and UE5). More utility = more people who want said ship  This is all to say I'm not really convinced ships will just tank nonstop. Some of this might seem obvious but thought I'd add my thoughts either way

author: 𝐑𝐎𝐌𝐄 | Virtuwul [ROME]
content: To bullet 2, I still think it is a great strategy to have the team develop the GAO/v1.0  of any new ship release. Player base buys up those ships. Those ships come with some kind of special NFT characteristic,  and the blueprints are released into the economy for guilds who then build V2 versions of those ships with various mod iterations and compete with other ship building guilds for customers  This will allow for: 1) the team to generate revenue from OG V1  ship sales for each release cycle and help define the future of ship blueprints 2) create original value ships that are irreplaceable. I'm potentially fine with burning up a guild constructed C9 in the HRZ, but not an OG C9. I'm going to want to protect that thing 3) move ship building and selling / competitive pricing to the market for a true supply and demand based capitalist market driven economy

author: [AEP] Boen
content:
I think my main concern with Bodhi is does he view the SA ecosystem experiment as 
'the best relative profit drive in the crypto space right now' or 
does he truly feel inspired to be part of the zeitgeist of the experiment? 

We all want profit, but I think most of us could make better returns elsewhere and are invested here because of the meta potential (in this case, expressed as a space based game as its driving force to develop the meta experience).I wouldn't care if he was a smaller player but he does have outsized impact. 
And I think any economic model that doesn't drive slightly higher ROI potential to the smallest players vs the largest players for the same input time of X, is likely to fail. 
I genuinely want to like Bodhi and hope that he feels welcome in this community. I know tensions are high and I think it is probably best if the team makes a tweak sooner than later.

content: Shifting Responsibility (Buck Passing): The speaker asserts that it is solely the team's responsibility to create checks and balances and improve the experience for all members. This could be considered a fallacy if the speaker, despite having significant influence due to substantial investments, distances themselves from any responsibility regarding the community's well-being or the project's direction.  Ad Hominem (Implying False Premises): The speaker dismisses the questions asked as based on "false premises" without addressing the actual content of the questions. This can be seen as avoiding the argument rather than engaging with it. The speaker claims that these premises (being responsible for the community and pretending to be altruistic) are inherently false without further explanation, which can be seen as an attempt to undermine the questioner's credibility or motives instead of directly addressing the points raised.  Appeal to Accomplishment: The speaker mentions spending "millions of dollars in assets" as a justification for having fulfilled their obligations to the project. This appeal suggests that financial contribution alone absolves the contributor of further responsibilities or scrutiny, which is not necessarily a sound argument, especially if the discussion involves ethical or communal responsibilities beyond financial input.  Circular Reasoning: The statement "We all pay our dues at the door when we buy assets" followed by "I paid my dues just like everyone else, when I spent millions of dollars in assets" may imply a circular logic where the premise (paying dues) is justified by itself (spending money as paying dues). It assumes the action of purchasing assets is both a necessary and sufficient contribution, without addressing other aspects of 'paying dues' like active participation or ethical engagement.  Ambiguity: The term "pay our dues" is somewhat ambiguous in this context. It is not clear whether this refers only to financial transactions or includes other forms of contribution and responsibility towards the community. This ambiguity can lead to misunderstandings or misinterpretations about the speaker's actual contributions and responsibilities.  Generalization: The speaker generalizes that their financial contribution equates to supporting the development of the project. This overlooks the nuanced reality that financial input does not automatically translate into positive or constructive contributions toward project development or community health.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content:
Straw Man Fallacy: Bodhi constructs a scenario where he implies the team might not want people to fully utilize their assets after selling them. Unless there is evidence that the team expressed such a sentiment, this might be a misrepresentation of the team’s intentions or rules, which can lead to a straw man argument. This fallacy occurs when someone argues against a position that the opponent doesn’t actually hold.

False Dilemma: Bodhi presents the situation as if there are only two choices—either the team allows full utilization of assets or they should not sell them at all. This simplifies what is likely a more complex issue, ignoring possible middle grounds or other nuanced solutions that could involve guidelines for using assets without completely restricting their use.

Appeal to Ridicule: By describing the expectation for asset users to consider self-sabotage of their earnings as "unreasonable," Bodhi is dismissing concerns about potential negative impacts on others as absurd without a substantive argument. This rhetorical technique can undermine legitimate discussion about how actions within the game impact its economy and other players.

Appeal to Wealth: Implicit in Bodhi’s argument is the idea that spending a large amount of money on assets entitles one to certain privileges or exemptions from criticism. This argument assumes that financial investment should directly translate to greater leverage or fewer restrictions, which is not inherently a just or sustainable policy in a balanced economic system.

Slippery Slope: Bodhi indirectly suggests that if some restrictions or expectations are placed on how assets are used, it might lead to players being asked to sacrifice their own benefits arbitrarily. This can be seen as a slippery slope argument where a small reasonable action (like some form of regulation) could supposedly lead to extreme outcomes without clear causal linkage.

author: GoldenLover | BubblePop
content: Your statement, "It’s not game breaking or they would have fixed it," presents a few logical fallacies that undermine the validity of your argument:  Circular Reasoning (Begging the Question): This fallacy is evident as Bodhi's conclusion that the issue is not game-breaking is based on the assumption that if it were, it would have already been fixed. This reasoning goes in a circle, as it assumes the premise (that the economy team fixes all game-breaking bugs promptly) to prove the conclusion (that the bug is not game-breaking).  False Cause (Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc): Bodhi implies a causal relationship between the economy team's inaction and the severity of the bug. He suggests that because the team hasn't fixed the bug, it must not be game-breaking. This fallacy occurs because he assumes that one event (the team's lack of action) necessarily follows from the other (the non-severity of the bug) without sufficient proof that this is always the case.  Hasty Generalization: This fallacy may be less directly apparent but is implicit in assuming that all significant bugs are quickly fixed by the team. Bodhi generalizes the team’s behavior or capability based on an unstated rule that all critical issues are promptly addressed, which may not always hold true depending on the circumstances like resource limitations, prioritization of tasks, or even awareness of the issue.  Appeal to Authority: While not explicitly stated, there's an underlying appeal to the authority of the economy team, suggesting that their inaction is a reliable indicator of the problem's severity. This can be fallacious if the team's capabilities, priorities, or strategies are not infallible or if they simply have different criteria for what constitutes a "game-breaking" issue.  tl;dr You are full of shit.

content: What are the crafting fees now? It was left for us to discover, but how can we tell if there's an error or simply confirm rates? author: 10^24 Stars
content:
Big gratz on selling out the crew presale in 24 hours.  Gonna chip in my opinion here on crew. 

The way I have imagined crew functioning is that they fulfill a certain career and there would be little point in training multiple roles instead of doubling down on a specialty, i.e. I will always have my best pilot doing piloting.  Any other aptitudes that the they have would be wasted.  Moving a character around in order to get XP in different roles sounds like a waste when they could continue to level their strongest aptitude and I could simply level a different crew in those other roles.  For someone playing with 100s of crew, the micro-management of moving around crew sounds intolerable.   I look forward to seeing the thinking behind the value of multiple aptitudes.

While I look forward to seeing how the team elucidates these issues, I was kind of thinking of a classic RPG attribute systems with primary attributes that are rolled based on the crew card rarity.  Those primary attributes then determine aptitudes. One could have a classic stats system with attributes like strength, intelligence, charisma, agility, etc.  Then the aptitudes would follow from that... for example command aptitude would be derived from intelligence and charisma,  flight would be derived from intelligence and agility,  engineering would be derived from intelligence and so on. Well, that is my 2 cents anyway

author: ! SH | Bohemian ⪛⦿⫺
content: Your argument is beyond making any sense and absolutely riddled with fallacies. I'm impressed you manage to pack them all in.   You keep attacking me even though Santi asked you to stop.  So here we go.  Here is how many fallacies your post contains. Saying that I only want to play passively like in Minecraft really misrepresents my point. This kind of Straw Man Fallacy oversimplifies my stance, making it easier to attack without addressing my actual concerns about fairness in gameplay coordination.  It has no bearing in the truth because saying I don't want to play the way Bodhi is playing doesn't mean I immediately want to play passive.  There's also a False Dichotomy here. The idea that if I don’t like the way the game is currently played, I should just leave and find a different game ignores the possibility that I might want to improve aspects of this game while still enjoying its core mechanics.  Plus, when you attack my character by calling my mentality "toxic" and "poor," you’re diving into an Ad Hominem attack. This shifts the focus from my valid points to a personal attack on me, which doesn’t really help the discussion.  You also seem to rely on an Appeal to Tradition and simplification, suggesting because Bodhi's move involves coordination and strategic moves that implies are how the game "should" be played, and thus my complaints are invalid. Just because something has always been done a certain way doesn’t mean it’s the best or only way to do it.  Another point is the False Cause fallacy, where you imply that those who take big risks and spend a lot of time are unfairly criticized solely for those reasons. But my criticism is more about the fairness of their tactics, not the effort they put in.  The argument also Generalizes by saying all complaints come from being outplayed and being sore losers, without recognizing that I might have legitimate concerns about game balance or fairness.  Then there’s a Red Herring when you defend Bodhi’s character and label me as a sore loser, which diverts attention from the real issues being discussed—like the tactics and coordination in the game.  Lastly, there's a bit of a Slippery Slope when you suggest that complaining about gameplay will lead to everyone complaining all the time, similar to an exaggerated scenario in esports. This assumes that one complaint will lead to a dramatic chain of events without any evidence.  Overall, these logical fallacies really undermine your argument and avoid engaging constructively with my valid concerns about how the game is being played.

author: ROME | Earther [ROME]
content:
Allow me to offer and analogy for the discussion above (and I'd truly like to know if you think it applies).

Say a really smart and cool group of people invited a bunch of friends to their awesome pad to have a fun pizza party. However, the pizza is really good and really expensive. So, to pay for it the hosts thought it would be fun to have guests pay for the size of their pizza plate, assuming most people will get a normal size for themselves or maybe medium if they're really hungry.  But some guests could buy a super expensive mega-sized plate (all-you-can-eat) if they wanted to. Cool. Helps pay for the party.
Each guest can then get a slice or two of pizza according to their plate size. Cool. Everyone can have a good time.

But what if some dude bought the mega-plate and piled it full of more pizza than he needed - more than he could eat. And what if they only had a limited amount of pizza at the party. That means people who came later got a plate with maybe one slice of pizza or maybe none!

Then mega-plate dude (with a huge pile of pizza) plops down on the couch with a big grin and is like, "Damn, this is an awesome party right?!" 

Others next to him smile politely and nibble on their one slice. Others cheer him on cause he was so smart and got the big plate. It's funny!

Others, though, look at those who got less pizza than they anticipated. They see hungry people at the party and this dude with a giant plate, and they criticize mega-plate dude for his party foul.

It's a party foul to take more than you need from a community of friends.

It makes the party less fun for others.

Hope that makes sense. (sorry for the long post - it came to me while mowing the lawn and I had to share)

P.S. Others also bought the mega-plate but saw limited supply of pizza and did not load up.

author: [AEP] Boen
content: It creates a parallel economic / market model where the team can continue to create original blueprint ships that people can pay extra for because they have mod bonus plus rarity of capped supply plus therefore collector status, and the team can then immediately allow for the guilds to start producing the same blueprints (call it 6 months after GAO release) and not really worry about guild ship manufacturing replacing team sales, versus the guilds have to wait a longer period of time to be able to build ships from available blueprints

author: [AEP] Boen
content:
It also allows for smaller players with less capital to access higher level ships but at lower cost points than GAO. So if a small player can only afford up to a XXS GAO ship, they could potentially afford a S or M guild ship. This opens up player base access wo feeling 'left out' because of an expensive NFT revenue model.
This allows guilds greater sales volume (team and DAO can take a % of the guild ship sales).

author: [AEP] Boen
content: GAO ships can't be destoryed in HRZ but have a long respawn time (ie, you still have to be careful with titan and commander GAO ship loss in HRZ because while those are respawning, your faction / guild may have a combat power vacuum for the enemy to take advantage of). Guild built ships can be perma destroyed in HRZ, and though emotions may be heated over it, I really think it would serve to cool things off because buyers are basically buying a ship intended to be burned at some point.

author: SW4GN3R [STAR]
content: Its pretty awesome.  But mostly because I'm already contributing a TON.    I'm unclear on how much it will change gameplay though. People are mostly contributing what they can based on their fleets/profits. Either they can afford to upkeep food, or not. (Or they are leeches)  e.g. I'm contributing a lot to keep my production going, only at the Starbase I'm using.  Smaller players who can't ship in food/toolkits probably wouldn't be able to take advantage of this mechanic.  So if this is incentive for smaller players to upkeep... I'd say it probably wont do anything because they already can't upkeep.  On the other hand if you are trying to make upkeeping some sort of business or encourage larger players to upkeep more Starbases, or just to reward those already doing a lot of upkeep..  It has a lot of promise.  Would this sort of venture encourage me to upkeep multiple Starbases?  If the numbers were tuned right i suppose.  EXP is a nice carrot because we are getting a tangible benefit that isn't costing anyone any money.  e.g. I really have no desire to do the SDU loop but I went out and bought a Rayfam for the exp.  I don't even care about the SDUs.

author: [SH]b0b [STAR]
content: Here's a breakdown of why auto converting the LP to Atlas will be so huge.  Right now, the bigger multi-faction players are accumulating LP by mass dumping high tier components into multiple factions and then slowly dripping the LP to maximize Atlas.  Once LP to Atlas auto-conversion is active, the effect will be:  Much higher variance in LP which means: HUGE days and then much lower days. We will have huge days when opportunities like Field Stabilizers open up and get aggressively installed.  This will also crush their earnings per component (which is good for the smaller players).  This will also discourage faction hopping a notch since they know they'll be competing with people in that faction.  Here's the big one: We will much lower days on other days which gives smaller players much better earnings on the majority of days.  Will dramatically nerf the mass dumpers long term earnings. Right now, many players are saving up LP and earning a good portion daily across all factions.  That will be over.  They will earn a massive amount 1 day... and then if they moves, he will earn ZERO.  And FYI: this was the original game design.  You can read it in the Sage Manual for reference

author: Eoganacht | BULK [BULK]
content: i hear you. I still think there should be a distinction between 'investments' in the game, which are GAO ships, vs burnable assets, which are guild built ships off those same GAO blueprints. you can tell your friends that BOTH of these still have significant asset cost. GAO ship destruction will have a heavy time and respawn cost element probably in the thousands of usd for commander level ships. I think traditional gamers would be impressed by that value loss component.  Guild built ships would also have a significant cost element to them, for example like $15K for a commander. that is still a hell of a lot of pain that traditional gamers would be flabbergasted over.  There is no real 'middle ground'. By creating a distinction between team GAO ships vs guild built ships, you are creating two parallel economic loops. Frankly I think it is a mistake to have guild built ships that can eventually flood the market, depending on market dynamics, with those ships having the same stats as a GAO ship. This takes away the finite element of the GAO ships.

The model I described that facilitates both value retention for GAO ships and lower pricing for crafted ships would work well imo. Plus GAO ships then become collector's items. And something new players could strive for. I disagree that newer players would feel like they missed out. If they save the funds, they can ultimately buy one of the GAO ships from a legacy holder too. In the meantime, they'd have a much lower entry point.   The big problem would be establishing the balance of their economic production outside of HRZ.

author: 𝕘𝕣𝕚𝕤𝕥
content:
(wrote my thoughts yesterday. community is awesome. love ya all. guess i’ll share this and it doesn’t matter because it’s clear the decision has been made) 

if GAO ships are on a cool down, if the cool down can be decreased by spending atlas 

>this will be considered the ultimate P2W

the price of GAO ships will balloon and become mythical to players. but not in a good way. they will feel only “lucky” OGs or whales can own them. one small set won’t face total loss. and even if the cool down is restrictive knowing it can be minimized by spending money? 

even if all ships are on a respawn cool down and no total loss in HRZ—the ability to respawn faster with atlas will be considered P2W

we already have a marketing problem. millions of gamers think web3 gaming is a joke and predatory. so they fall in love with new internet spaceships and owning assets and a player run economy but….learn that some ships are indestructible? that the penalty can be paid off? how do you think that will go down?

it’s stupid to express this position when the ceo floated the idea and many high vwap players cheered it on. i’m a low vwap player from a dissolved guild but i want this game to prosper and walking away from the one thing that made it different? intriguing? i think it’s foolish without even trying. let’s at least try to realize the founding vision of the HRZ

if you don’t want to lose your ships, stay out of the HRZ. but if you want to go for the highest reward in game—why would one group be able to do so without ever risking their OG ships? why would such a thing be possible for players lucky enough or wealthy enough (when they inflate in price) to own a GAO ship?

author: Xap✨ [STAR]
content:
@SW4GN3R I am a supporter of full destruction in HRZ. Mainly it is just feels so exciting and sweaty. That said I can see the argument that having Gao ships to have a respawn will make HRZ more attractive and generate a lot more economic flow. 

There has been some very good conversations here already for both sides. Here is an expansion on those suggestions:

GAO ships come with a "respawn Module" by default. Activating this respawn after destruction is very expensive and time consuming.,
Crafted ships are flyable without a respawn module. However this module can be constructed but it is very costly to construct. This will make all ships at the same level.,
There is a deep HRZ zone (near IRIS?) where all ship can be destroyed without an opportunity of respawn. The respawn becomes disabled due to Cosmic currents. The destroyed GAO ship will get a memory plate instead for keepsake but the ship is gone. Forever.,
Hence there is a very limited area in HRZ where you should not venture if you do not want to loose your ship. Period. Meanwhile you can experience all the other HRZ activity if you are willing to take the risk and to pay for it.,

author: Xap✨ [STAR]
content: There is an argument to stay in MRZ. However I feel there are activities in HRZ that are highly desirable and making it limited is not smart.,

content: There's a can of HRZ worms that no one has opened up and you're the perfect guy to theory craft on it.  And this might be the biggest problem.  The risk/reward ratios of the HRZ and their potential economic impact.  First let's forget all the HRZ "I want life or death battles" for a minutes.  Let's imagine there's a 20% survival rate for the average player who spends a week in the HRZ.  What does the REWARDS need to be like for the ODDS to make sense?  As a poker player, you understand pot odds.    If the pot isn't juicy enough in relation to your odds... you probably fold (unless you're trying to bluff).  The rewards need to be INSANELY strong... almost absurd for a player to enter the HRZ.  NOW... What happens if a hyper aggressive whale TAKES over the HRZ?  Probably an economic disaster for the rest of the players due to the fact that the rewards would be astronomical.  Your turn... GO

author: 𝐑𝐎𝐌𝐄 | Virtuwul [ROME]
content: It had nothing to do with the Titan sales. In fact I brought up that topic before any of the titan sales happened. I'm hesitant to open this conversation back up, since it is years away from materialization (most likely). When I presented the idea, I had been thinking about the success of nullsec in Eve.  A key reason pvp was so prominent was that the psychological barrier of losing assets was low. The ships/fleets didn't have real monetary value, for one, and they were easy enough to craft and replace in most cases. So, the TLDR of what I presented is this:  Two-class ship system: GAO vs. Crafted Under this model, crafting requirements could be drastically reduced, making ship construction faster and easier,Also implies higher turnover for those players looking to participate in ship manufacturing as an econ loop,Shorter time between cash flows for ship manufacturers / and higher (presumable) demand,This would naturally put downward pressure on all ship assets (not acceptable),The lifetime insurance on GAO assets supports prices trading higher than a standard crafted ship,The GAO assets become aspirational targets for new players,However, crafted ships perform equally in HRZ to any GAO asset,Challenge: need to reconcile how those crafted ships perform in MRZ/SZ, given we could see massive inflation in crafted ships that would need to perform worse in non-HRZ territory, Benefits: New players have a lower barrier to entry and smaller up-front investment to get into the game,Enables us to reach a more mainstream audience that won't likely ever buy a $100,000+ game asset,Creates more activity in the HRZ because perception of risk is lower for most,Ensures we have less possibility of short term distortions in economic output (inflation),It's not P2W, because new players can literally enter the game for less than our OGs. OGs benefit from lifetime insurance, and those assets are desirable to many people who want that lifetime insurance perk, Ultimately I was trying to identify a path to balancing incentive structure in HRZ so we don't see short term control leading to hyperinflation (as we need to make HRZ quite attractive to justify risking very expense ships). Under this model, the rewards in HRZ could be more in line with our original proposal of 8x, instead of something like 100x (my own estimate). Separately, the dichotomy in ship types also speeds up manufacturing times and turnover, which is good for manufacturers. Instead of waiting 6-9 months for a large ship craft, it could be weeks. And then further supporting more activity in HRZ given the lower risk profile of burner ships.  I'd envision a lot of players using those crafted ships as burners in HRZ, and anchoring those fleets with their GAO ships.  Again, all theory crafting from my own side. Nothing decided at the team level, and a lot of internal pressure to stick to how we originally presented the HRZ in the white paper.

author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content:
I personally understand the perspective of people saying the OG ships could look like P2W if there is no destruction in HRZ. However, Michael explained pretty well how you could balance that aspect. If some OG wants to cash out with his/her GAO ship, he/she can do it, sell the ships, and build new ships which can be destroyed.

What concerns me, from a pure gameplay perspective, is having a completely empty HRZ where only a few people will go. You are basically cutting off a nice portion of Galia due to fear of losing assets. Assuming new ships will be much cheaper, you cannot compare OG ships to newly built ships either way. You either keep the price for shipbuilding high (or at least comparable to the price of GAO ships) or the ones who will be "disadvantaged" will be the OGs who bought ships at higher prices (even though I admit they would have had time to recover from their initial investment over time).

author: The Only SignalONI
content: Hey Mike! I seem to recall Stealth is among the features the team expects to implement last. And on that point, at present any form of true stealth is not possible with the current state of affairs on Solana. It would either require a private L2 to run on top of Solana, or some off-chain logic operated by the team that would function like a layer in between Solana and the players. Neither is an optimal solution, but hopefully the future will make it clear which direction is best (or if there is somehow a 3rd option). Until that time this game will remain a lot like chess: everything is visible.  As to SAGE, the team could of course give ships with stealth some sort of bonus in combat. They will likely do the same for some of the stats that do not function practically just yet.

author: Xcode [STAR]
content: I know this isn't one of the options we're discussing, but I'd like to say this anyway: I believe that PvE can be more engaging for the majority of players. I'm very afraid that PvP, with such a big difference in players' wallets, might further create "fear" of playing and push the majority of players into LRZ, while only those with a significant fleet can engage in PvP maneuvers. Although many players find PvE boring, there are many more players who completely avoid PvP because they prefer a more "peaceful" experience. With that being said, I think territory control can certainly be an incentive and even appealing, but the way the current upgrade system is designed, it's really too punitive. If an SB at level 3 is reset to 0, months of scanned SDUs are lost (for the current economy).

content: @Lysimach | Make Polis Great ⁠archived-foundation-room⁠ Crew simulation needs to be realistic. author: [HEIM] SDU pimpUstur
content: At the very least, make efficiency a stat that you need to look for in crew. This would make crew shopping/upgrading an interesting activity. author: [HEIM] SDU pimpUstur

author: [HEIM] SDU pimpUstur
content: The main issue is the obvious disparity of efficiency distribution. As it is right now, it is unlikely that a whale is operating as efficiently as a smaller player, the main problem is that a smaller player gets eaten up by fees with the current systems in place. So a bigger player's portion of the proverbial pie keeps getting bigger due to the fact a small player struggles purely because of fees. Ultimately this is the problem that needs to be solved. If everyone is operating at exactly the same efficiency, then nobody has an advantage over anyone, but that is obviously not the case here. I would argue that forcibly enabling efficiency penalties to larger players (in a realistic way, for example, diminishing returns on crew), this would help diminish a whale's overall increasing his portion of the pie, and subsequently allowing smaller players to harvest more of the pie for themselves provided they were doing things efficiently.

author: [AEP] Moustacheride
content: One reason the numbers were released now was to get a bit of community feedback prior to going live. It's possible we tweak the numbers some before the feature launches. The transports are getting something like a 2x base transport capacity, which is similar to spec perks for other features. But Chip and I can take a look at the balance between spec & modules. The passenger modules may have a little more weight right now relative to base specs than the cargo/fuel/ammo.  Also, think of the transports more for moving crew around and leaving them there for a bit to work. And likely needing to take multiple trips if you have a lot of crew. It's not really meant to be an entire mobile crafting unit that shows up, stays & crafts, and then leaves with all of the crew. The transport can leave the passenger crew there and go do other stuff. (and later being able to do p2p crew transport and transport related missions)  Transport ships also more base cargo space than the combat ships, so they have a more non-combat utility in that way as well. The end goal is to make all the specs balanced.  Thanks for the feedback!

author: [HEIM] SDU pimpUstur
content: giving incentives for whales to upkeep starbases is a good thing, not a bad thing. Remember, whales only get the crafting fees, if someone is crafting there. This gives room for things like sanctions and boycotting, which is kinda cool, IMHO. providing food to a starbase is a cost of business, shifting that focus to the whale instead of the little guy, is good, not bad. The small player would have to pay the crafting fee either way. and it's doubtful that whales will just run around spam filling starbases with food thinking they will rake in all the fees, because they could well just run themselves into the ground doing that (if nobody uses their crafting windows). They will have to advertise, and make sure either they themselves are using the crafting window, or ensure that other people are using it.

author: Space Bull
content:
@[AEP] Angorian 
I run into this and think about this often as well.  It’s especially challenging because, as we all know, nothing quite like Star Atlas exists.  So there’s no direct comparison or example that quite covers all the important differences between SA and a “game”.

To make things more difficult, we’re in development stages.  Things are changing constantly, and the big picture isn’t all that clear unless one really has the time and interest to take it all in.

That said, I usually start from a very top down, simplified view of the SA “Platform”, focusing on the fundamental pillars of gameplay, how they interact and exist in the same “universe” and most importantly, with a real world economy and true asset ownership.
Then I usually zoom in from there and start focusing on the proprietary technologies and all of the areas in which we’re “pioneering”.. so like UE5 graphics, MetaGravity, no load screens, benefits of blockchain, etc.

Thinking overall, once we have a viral game loop, friends explaining it to friends via word of mouth will be the most effective.

author: [HEIM] SDU pimpUstur
content:
@Xcode a scenario, if you will:

There are 185,867,386/194,664,862 power sources in a starbase. Medium player A with $20k worth of assets and 1k crew puts an install of 10 million PS to finish up the starbase. Hypothetically, this install will take 15 hours, let's say. Player A uses his own toolkits, and gets the job going.

Whale player B comes along with $1 million of assets, sees through eveeye that there is an upgrade in progress, but knows that because he is a phat nugget, decides to use his 50k crew, and massive freighter fleets to in less than 15 hours not only transport 10 million powersources, but also uses his 50k crew to complete the craft in 3 hours.

Player A is furious because even being a medium player, with decent assets, has been conned out of his toolkits, and the time and effort it took him to get 10 million power sources to the starbase in the first place, and now has to look somewhere else to upgrade.

this is how unbalanced this system is currently.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: Morning.  I only think that works as a balance for smaller and larger players if the toolkits required aren't based on a time component but a quantity of units to use for upgrade.   The game needs a mechanism that can work for minnows and whales alike. Toolkit burn based on time means that minnows are dependent on whales to keep an SB going, and therefore whales have more power in determining SB upgrade timing, esp for juicy components like FS.  If the toolkits utilized is based on the unit count for the upgrade (like FS units), then minnows are not dependent on whales to fund an SB, and both minnows and whales would need to move an appropriate amount of toolkits to fund their upgrade. And frankly toolkit use based on units used for an upgrade makes more practical sense then a time based burn mechanism.  This means whales and minnows alike are needing to provide their requisite toolkit amount. And you could build the burn mechanism in a manner where there is a slight increase in toolkit burn usage on a per unit basis, the more units you are upgrading.

author: The Man | RomeONI
content:
I'm not in a rush, just want to make sure they consider it along the way. The complaints people have about whales taking so much larger of a piece than their investment would indicate are a symptom of how the game is setup, not the root problem. So I am trying to point out root problems as well as possible fixes so they can plan ahead for the next iteration. If the game isn't just a math simulation then it becomes harder for one person to extract a ton, and easier for someone who is good at whatever game to do better even with a small investment.
